evidence.quote: The proportions of CCM genes (KRIT1 69.2%, CCM2 15.4%, and PDCD10 15.4%) affected were similar to those in previous reports. 12 However, the patients without detected mutations accounted for a larger proportion (38.1%) of our cohort, in contrast to previous cohorts in which mutations were undetected in >5% of the patients. These patients had at least five lesions and no history of head, neck, or intracranial radiation, suggesting clinical FCCM. There are several reasons that mutations were not detected. First, intronic variants or copy number variations in KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10 could not be detected by our DNA sequencing method. In fact, large deletion/duplication mutations, such as deletions spanning exons 2-10, accounted for 30-60% of CCM2 variants despite a low proportion (approximately 20%) of CCM2 variants. 13 , 14 Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification and whole genome sequencing are needed to identify these variants. Second, other gene mutations could induce FCCM despite the rarity of the disease. F. Gianfrancesco et al. proposed that ZPLD1 mutation is associated with FCCM. 15 Furthermore, various genes related to CCM pathophysiology were recently discovered. 2 In the 2-hit model, biallelic LOF in CCM genes, achieved by one somatic mutation in heterozygous germline mutation or two somatic mutations in wild-type gene, is required to initiate CCM formation. Moreover, gain-of-function (GOF) mutations in MAP3K3, encoding MEKK3, have been confirmed in sporadic CCM patients. 16 LOF in CCM genes and GOF in MAP3K3 are mutually exclusive, and the researchers suggested that CCM complexes suppress the activity of MEKK3. Therefore, the mutation of these genes could be a novel cause of FCCM. Finally, multiple sporadic CCMs are possible but rare.

evidence.quote: Cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) is an intracranial vascular malformation causing a collection of abnormally distended capillaries. 1 CCM is broadly divided into sporadic and familial categories. Familial CCM (FCCM) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in three genes, KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10. In contrast to sporadic CCM patients, who typically have a solitary lesion, FCCM patients present with multiple CCM lesions showing progressive increases in number and size. The pathophysiology of CCM has recently been elucidated, and various mechanisms associated with the development and hemorrhage have been suggested. 2 These prior studies demonstrated that the products of the three genes (KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10) are associated with CCM form complexes. Loss of function (LOF) of these genes leads to the formation of CCM. Despite the tremendous progress in understanding CCM, the explicit mechanisms underlying the vascular-specific manifestation and vascular malformation suppression of the three CCM genes remain unknown. Understanding variants in the CCM-associated genes could help explain the function of CCM complexes and their interaction with other proteins. 3 Hence, genetic testing for those suspected to be FCCM could be important. While many variants have been reported, studies on Korean FCCM patients are sparse. 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 Furthermore, previous studies paid little attention to analyzing the radiologic features and age-related disease burden according to the genes. We examined the manifestations of Korean FCCM patients and their CCM gene test results and evaluated the clinical and radiologic features associated with these mutations. In addition, the disease burden of FCCM according to age was analyzed.

evidence.section: Body / Methods / Clinical data and brain imaging
evidence.quote: We investigated the patients' clinical manifestations, including demographics, symptoms, presence of spinal cavernous malformation (CM) and cutaneous CM, history of cavernous angioma with symptomatic hemorrhage (CASH), brain surgery due to CCM, radiotherapy for other reasons, and tumors. We only reviewed brain MRIs, including T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and axial susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient echo imaging (GRE). For analysis, a total of eighty brain MRIs were conducted, and 20% (16/80) and 80% (64/80) were MRIs with GRE and SWI sequences, respectively. The last MRIs in all patients contained SWI sequences. For recording the location, we used the SWI because of its high sensitivity. However, we included not the lesions, which were only visible on SWI, but the lesions frankly visible on T1WI and T2WI (i.e., non-Zabramski type IV).

evidence.quote: A total of thirty-four patients underwent the CCM gene test. (Fig. 1) However, seven patients with multiple lesions were excluded because the lesions were regarded as non-CCM lesions, including cerebral microbleeds in small vessel disease (n = 5), diffuse axonal injury (n = 1), and multiple and recurrent intracerebral hemorrhages without CCM lesions (n = 1) by neuroradiologists. Of the remaining 27 patients, six sporadic CCM patients with a wild-type FCCM gene, a single CCM lesion, and no family history of CCM were excluded. The twenty-one FCCM patients were divided into two groups: thirteen patients with pathogenic variants in CCM genes and eight patients with undetected mutations. The eight patients had multiple lesions suggestive of FCCM. All (n = 21) of the patients considered to be FCCM (gene confirmed or clinical) were analyzed for clinical manifestation and radiologic findings (cohort 1). Furthermore, four family members of three probands underwent a family gene test and had the same mutation as the proband. The data of twenty-five patients, combining cohort 1 with the familial members, were used for the analysis of the age-related disease burden in FCCM (cohort 2). There was neither a patient with a developmental venous anomaly nor a history of radiation in our cohort.

evidence.section: Body / Result / Detailed clinical, genetic data, and age-related disease burden of gene-confirmed FCCM patients
evidence.quote: We investigated the detailed clinical and genetic information of the gene-confirmed FCCM individuals, including the proband and family members. (Table 2) The family members of one patient with a KRIT1 variant (K7), and two patients with PDCD10 variants (P1 and P2), received genetic testing, and four family members with the same variant as the proband were detected. Furthermore, these family members had CCM lesions confirmed by brain MRI. Two patients (K3 and P2) had spinal CM, and one (C1) had cutaneous CM. Among the probands with mutations detected, six experienced CASH. Two patients experienced recurrent symptomatic hemorrhage and severe neurological sequelae. In the KRIT1 variant group, two patients (22.2%) had splice-site mutations, and the others had protein-truncating variants. (Table S1) All of the mutations were null. The CCM2 group comprised one patient with a nonsense mutation and one with a missense mutation. The PDCD10 group included one patient with a nonsense mutation and one with a splice-site mutation. Interestingly, five novel variants and one novel variant were confirmed in KRIT1 and PDCD10, respectively. Four patients with KRIT1 variants had a history of tumor or a current tumor. One patient (K3) presented with headache and neck pain. Brain and spine MRI demonstrated CCM and spinal CM. At the age of 52 years, a follow-up spine MRI revealed an increased size and prominent heterogeneous enhancement of T2 high signal intensity around the CM in the thoracic spinal cord. The neuroradiologist suggested the possibility of CM with a recent hemorrhage and tumorous condition. The surgical biopsy exhibited diffuse midline glioma, classified as WHO grade IV.

evidence.quote: Cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) is an intracranial vascular malformation causing a collection of abnormally distended capillaries. 1 CCM is broadly divided into sporadic and familial categories. Familial CCM (FCCM) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in three genes, KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10. In contrast to sporadic CCM patients, who typically have a solitary lesion, FCCM patients present with multiple CCM lesions showing progressive increases in number and size. The pathophysiology of CCM has recently been elucidated, and various mechanisms associated with the development and hemorrhage have been suggested. 2 These prior studies demonstrated that the products of the three genes (KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10) are associated with CCM form complexes. Loss of function (LOF) of these genes leads to the formation of CCM. Despite the tremendous progress in understanding CCM, the explicit mechanisms underlying the vascular-specific manifestation and vascular malformation suppression of the three CCM genes remain unknown. Understanding variants in the CCM-associated genes could help explain the function of CCM complexes and their interaction with other proteins. 3 Hence, genetic testing for those suspected to be FCCM could be important. While many variants have been reported, studies on Korean FCCM patients are sparse. 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 Furthermore, previous studies paid little attention to analyzing the radiologic features and age-related disease burden according to the genes. We examined the manifestations of Korean FCCM patients and their CCM gene test results and evaluated the clinical and radiologic features associated with these mutations. In addition, the disease burden of FCCM according to age was analyzed.

evidence.quote: Cohort 1 consisted of nine patients with KRIT1 variants, two with CCM2 variants, two with PDCD10 variants, and eight with the mutation not detected (Table 1). In Table 1, clinical characteristics and imaging findings are described according to All, KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10, Mutation detected, and Mutation not detected groups. The mean diagnosis ages of the overall and the last brain MRI were 36.8 (standard deviation, SD 18.5) and 45.0 (SD 18.5) years old, respectively. There was a slight female predominance (male: female = 38.1:61.9). A total of 90.5% of the patients were symptomatic, and seizures were the most common manifestation. Moreover, the mean age of seizure onset was 34.5 (SD 19.5) years. CASH occurred in 52.4% of the patients overall; the mean age of CASH was 29.4 (SD 18.8) years old, and the mean number of CASH events was 1.8 (SD 1.3). Overall, 33.3% of the patients underwent surgery for CASH or enlarged symptomatic CCM lesions. A total of 42.9% of the overall patients had a family history. However, the rate was inaccurate because the family history of CCM was usually obtained by history taking. Meanwhile, the lesions were distributed over various locations. The frequencies were lower in the basal ganglia (9.5%) and thalamus (42.9%) than in the other sites.

evidence.quote: We investigated the detailed clinical and genetic information of the gene-confirmed FCCM individuals, including the proband and family members. (Table 2) The family members of one patient with a KRIT1 variant (K7), and two patients with PDCD10 variants (P1 and P2), received genetic testing, and four family members with the same variant as the proband were detected. Furthermore, these family members had CCM lesions confirmed by brain MRI. Two patients (K3 and P2) had spinal CM, and one (C1) had cutaneous CM. Among the probands with mutations detected, six experienced CASH. Two patients experienced recurrent symptomatic hemorrhage and severe neurological sequelae. In the KRIT1 variant group, two patients (22.2%) had splice-site mutations, and the others had protein-truncating variants. (Table S1) All of the mutations were null. The CCM2 group comprised one patient with a nonsense mutation and one with a missense mutation. The PDCD10 group included one patient with a nonsense mutation and one with a splice-site mutation. Interestingly, five novel variants and one novel variant were confirmed in KRIT1 and PDCD10, respectively. Four patients with KRIT1 variants had a history of tumor or a current tumor. One patient (K3) presented with headache and neck pain. Brain and spine MRI demonstrated CCM and spinal CM. At the age of 52 years, a follow-up spine MRI revealed an increased size and prominent heterogeneous enhancement of T2 high signal intensity around the CM in the thoracic spinal cord. The neuroradiologist suggested the possibility of CM with a recent hemorrhage and tumorous condition. The surgical biopsy exhibited diffuse midline glioma, classified as WHO grade IV.

evidence.quote: A total of thirty-four patients underwent the CCM gene test. (Fig. 1) However, seven patients with multiple lesions were excluded because the lesions were regarded as non-CCM lesions, including cerebral microbleeds in small vessel disease (n = 5), diffuse axonal injury (n = 1), and multiple and recurrent intracerebral hemorrhages without CCM lesions (n = 1) by neuroradiologists. Of the remaining 27 patients, six sporadic CCM patients with a wild-type FCCM gene, a single CCM lesion, and no family history of CCM were excluded. The twenty-one FCCM patients were divided into two groups: thirteen patients with pathogenic variants in CCM genes and eight patients with undetected mutations. The eight patients had multiple lesions suggestive of FCCM. All (n = 21) of the patients considered to be FCCM (gene confirmed or clinical) were analyzed for clinical manifestation and radiologic findings (cohort 1). Furthermore, four family members of three probands underwent a family gene test and had the same mutation as the proband. The data of twenty-five patients, combining cohort 1 with the familial members, were used for the analysis of the age-related disease burden in FCCM (cohort 2). There was neither a patient with a developmental venous anomaly nor a history of radiation in our cohort.
